notes: The Hebrew calls Jehoshaphat king of Israel here, though his kingdom was Judah. Azariah and Azariahu represent two closely related forms of a name in this list.
The final phrase names chariot commanders but does not explicitly identify their side. The account does not say that Edom was brought back under Judah’s rule.
The text attributes this letter to Elijah. It gives no explanation of its timing in relation to the Elijah narratives in Kings.
Jehoahaz is called Ahaziah in 22:1 and Azariah in 22:6. The different forms are retained where they occur.
The funeral burning was an honor for the dead; the verse does not say that his body would have been cremated. Compare 16:14.
vocabulary: Lamp
The lamp image represents the continuing life of David’s royal house.
Prostitution
Here the image describes abandoning the LORD for other gods. It should not be read as an additional report about sexual conduct.

notes: The pinned Hebrew reads forty-two. This conflicts with the preceding account of his father’s age; 2 Kings 8:26 reads twenty-two. The discrepancy is retained, not resolved silently. Daughter of Omri can indicate a later-generation descendant.
Jehoram and Joram are forms of the same name here. Verse 6 calls Judah’s king Azariah, although the surrounding account calls him Ahaziah; compare Jehoahaz in 21:17.
The Hebrew says son of Jehoshaphat, using son for a descendant. The capture in Samaria and subsequent killing are retained as this account gives them.
vocabulary: Anointed
Set apart for a task by anointing; Jehu’s commission concerns the destruction of Ahab’s house.
Jehoshabeath
The rescuer is both Ahaziah’s sister and the priest Jehoiada’s wife. Her actions preserve Joash’s life.

notes: The order to kill an entrant concerns unauthorized entry during this guarded installation. The preceding verse permits priests and serving Levites to enter.
Testimony may refer to a written covenant or law document associated with the king’s obligations. The object is not described further here.
Pillar may designate a pillar or a raised standing place associated with the king.
The Hebrew names Jehoiada himself, the people, and the king as the covenant parties here.
The Hebrew places priests and Levites together without a conjunction. Levitical priests follows that wording; priests and Levites is another possible understanding.
vocabulary: Holy
Set apart for the LORD’s service; the access rule concerns the sanctuary.
Unclean
A ritual condition that restricts sanctuary access, not a claim of inferior human worth.

notes: The sentence is understood as Jehoiada arranging two marriages for Joash.
The levy recalls the contribution for the wilderness sanctuary; compare Exodus 30:11–16.
Clothed preserves the Hebrew image of God’s Spirit coming upon Zechariah for his prophetic speech.
The Hebrew says sons of Jehoiada, although this chapter has named one murdered son, Zechariah. The plural is retained.

The difficult phrase rendered many pronouncements can also be understood in terms of a heavy burden or tribute. Exposition renders midrash, an account or interpretation, without identifying it with a later literary work.
vocabulary: Loyal love
Hesed: committed kindness within a relationship. Joash’s failure to remember it drives the account’s accusation.
Call to account
The dying appeal asks the LORD to see the killing and require an answer for it.

notes: The abrupt Hebrew imperatives are followed by a warning of defeat. They can be heard as a challenge: go ahead and rely on military strength, but God can bring you down. Other readings understand a conditional contrast with going without the hired troops.
The men thrown from the cliff are living captives. The text reports their killing in explicit bodily terms.
Samaria is retained in the geographical span, although its relation to Judah’s cities is difficult.
Jehoahaz is another form used for Ahaziah in this royal family; compare 21:17 and 22:1.
The Hebrew reads city of Judah. City of David is familiar from related burial notices and from the Kings parallel, but is not substituted here.
vocabulary: Each for his own sin
The quotation limits punishment of children for their fathers’ offenses; compare Deuteronomy 24:16.
Talent
An ancient unit of weight. The hundred talents here measure silver paid for the hired troops.
Cubit
A length based on the forearm, roughly half a meter; four hundred cubits is an approximate modern distance of two hundred meters.

notes: The pinned wording concerns seeing God and is rendered visions of God. A different reading yields instruction in the fear of God. The verse does not identify this Zechariah with a better-known prophet.
Jeiel follows the source’s read form; the written name is Jeuel.
The text describes designed devices for arrows and stones but does not give enough detail to identify their mechanism.
The Hebrew tsaraat names a serious skin condition with ritual consequences. It is not a precise diagnosis of modern leprosy.
Separate house interprets a difficult expression associated with freedom or exemption. The following clause makes exclusion from the LORD’s house explicit.
vocabulary: Heart grew proud
Literally, his heart became high. Strength gives way to self-exaltation in the narrative.
Censer
A vessel used for burning incense.

notes: The exception recalls Uzziah’s entry to burn incense in 26:16–21.
The same tribute is reported for three years. The silver and grain amounts are retained in their ancient units.
vocabulary: Ophel
A raised area of Jerusalem associated with its fortifications.
Kor
An ancient dry measure for grain; the precise modern equivalent varies.

notes: This verse says that Ahaz burned his sons in the fire. The harm is explicit in the Hebrew.
The captives are kin of their captors. Oded challenges the plan to enslave them, and the account lists concrete acts of care before their return.
The Hebrew has kings of Assyria in the plural here, although one king is named in verse 20.
The title king of Israel is retained as written; Ahaz ruled Judah.
Tilgath-pilneser preserves the form of the Assyrian king’s name used here in Chronicles.
vocabulary: Baals
Baal can be a divine title or name; the plural here refers to the objects of this worship.
Men and women slaves
The Hebrew distinguishes male and female enslavement. Servants would obscure the coercion in this proposed action.

notes: The list names fourteen Levites in seven pairs. Jeiel in verse 13 and Jehiel in verse 14 follow the read forms in the source.
The work runs from the first through the sixteenth day of the first month. The following chapter explains the later Passover date.
Verse 21 groups four sets of seven animals together. The following actions distinguish the goats as the sin offering and repeat that the offerings are for all Israel.
The Hebrew says that God prepared for the people, without explicitly naming what he prepared.
vocabulary: Consecrate
Set apart for sacred service. Consecration of people and cleansing of the house prepare for renewed worship.
Atonement
The ritual addresses sin and restores the community’s relation to God; the repeated scope is all Israel.
Consecrated yourselves
Literally, filled your hands, an expression for dedication to service.
Well-being offerings
Sacrifices associated with fellowship, thanksgiving, and shared meals; the fat is offered on the altar.

notes: The second-month observance follows insufficient priestly preparation and the people’s absence. Compare the provision for a later Passover in Numbers 9:9–14.
In large numbers follows one understanding of the Hebrew. Another is for a long time.
The prayer does not deny the ritual shortfall. It asks for atonement for those seeking God, and the LORD is said to heal the people without a specific illness being named.
The final verb can express thanksgiving or confession. The festival context supports giving thanks, while the broader sense of acknowledging God remains relevant.
Levitical priests follows the linked Hebrew designation; priests and Levites is another possible understanding.
vocabulary: Give your hand
An image of yielding allegiance or pledging loyalty, paired here with the opposite image of a stiff neck.
One heart
Shared purpose expressed as a common heart.
Resident foreigners
People living among Israel or Judah without being native members of those communities; they share in the rejoicing.

notes: The tithe of sacred things is a compressed expression. The translation retains it rather than replacing it with another kind of offering.
Cananiah follows the source’s read form. The written form is commonly represented as Conaniah. The same choice is used in 35:9.

The distribution and registration instructions are compressed and difficult. Three years old is the Hebrew reading in verse 16; it is not changed to thirty. Verse 17 separately gives twenty as the Levite registration threshold. Household dependents are explicitly included in verse 18.
vocabulary: The LORD’s camps
The sanctuary precincts are pictured as the LORD’s encampment.
Firstfruits and tithe
The first yield offered to God and a tenth set apart from the produce. They are related but distinct terms.
Most holy gifts
Gifts subject to particular restrictions on their handling and use.

notes: Raised it to the towers follows one understanding of a difficult construction phrase. Other readings describe raising or erecting towers on the wall.
The pinned text says he guided them. A reading that gives them rest appears in some translations; it is not substituted here.
The sign is mentioned without description. The fuller accounts in Kings and Isaiah supply details that this verse does not repeat.
The statement that God left Hezekiah to test him and know his heart is retained without explaining away its wording.
The burial location can be understood as the ascent to the tombs or their upper area.
vocabulary: Millo
A named fortification or earthwork associated with the City of David.
Arm of flesh
An image of mortal, human strength; it is contrasted with the LORD’s help.
Language of Judah
The local language understood by the people on Jerusalem’s wall.

notes: Made his sons pass through the fire is the source’s wording for the sacrificial practice. It should not be taken to describe a harmless ceremony; compare the explicit burning in 28:3.
Hooks is retained without specifying their placement on Manasseh’s body. The destination is Babylon, although his captors serve Assyria’s king.
Rebuilt follows the read form. The written form means established or prepared.
Hozai follows the name as pointed in the Hebrew. Another understanding takes the word as a reference to seers. The prayer mentioned here is not quoted in this chapter.
vocabulary: Host of heaven
The heavenly array, including sun, moon, and stars, treated here as objects of worship.
Humbled himself
Brought himself low before God. Its repetition distinguishes Manasseh’s later response from Amon’s refusal.

sections.29: The covenant is read and renewed

notes: Ruins follows the read form of a difficult Hebrew expression.
The read form says they returned to Jerusalem; the written form can be read as and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. This draft follows the read form and retains the resulting repetition of location.
Poured out refers to handling the collected silver or money. The verb can also be used for melting; this account does not describe minting coins.
Huldah is a woman exercising prophetic authority. Tokhath represents the read form תָּקְהַת; the written form is תוקהת.

The promise of burial in peace stands beside Josiah’s later fatal battle wound in 35:23–24. The accompanying explanation is that he will not see the coming disaster on this place; the tension is not removed.
vocabulary: Law
Torah: instruction given through Moses. The discovered book is also called the book of the covenant in verse 30.
Tender heart
A responsive heart, shown here in humility, torn clothes, and tears.
Testimonies
Covenant instructions or stipulations, listed alongside commands and statutes.

notes: The command to place the ark in the house does not explain where it had been or why. No removal story is supplied.
Cananiah follows the read form, consistently with 31:12–13.
The Hebrew uses the same general cooking verb for the Passover over the fire and the other sacred offerings in vessels. The fire description is retained; compare Exodus 12:8–9.
Neco first claims that God has sent him; verse 22 itself describes Neco’s words as from God’s mouth. The translation keeps both levels of attribution.
This account places the journey to Jerusalem before the report of Josiah’s death. It is not rewritten to match the wording of 2 Kings 23:29–30.
The Laments is the collection named by the text. It need not be identified with the biblical book now called Lamentations. Male and female singers are both explicitly present.
vocabulary: Passover offerings
The lambs and young goats provided for the Passover meal; the cattle are separately counted.
Lament
A formal expression of mourning. Here Josiah’s death becomes part of continuing communal remembrance.
